entry: Hard science fiction novel by Chinese author Liu Cixin, the first book in the *Remembrance of Earth's Past* trilogy. It opens during the [[Cultural Revolution]], when astrophysicist Ye Wenjie broadcasts a secret message that draws a reply from the alien planet Trisolaris, which lies in a system of three Sun-like stars, a representative example of the [[Three-body problem]] in [[Orbital mechanics]]. The English translation by Ken Liu (2014) was the first novel by an Asian writer to win a Hugo Award for Best Novel. An English-language [[Netflix]] series adaptation, *3 Body Problem*, was released in 2024.

French historical adventure novel by [[Alexandre Dumas]], written with ghostwriter Auguste Maquet and first serialized in 1844. It is the first of Dumas's three *d'Artagnan Romances* and belongs to the swashbuckler genre, with heroic swordsmen who fight for justice. Set between 1625 and 1628, it follows the young d'Artagnan, who leaves home in Gascony for Paris hoping to join the Musketeers of the Guard. He is befriended by three of the most formidable musketeers of the age, Athos, Porthos and Aramis. Dumas portrays many injustices and absurdities of the *Ancien Régime*, which gave the novel political resonance at a time when French republicans and monarchists were still in fierce debate. The story continues in *Twenty Years After* and *The Vicomte of Bragelonne: Ten Years Later*.

American [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] and comedy trio, active from 1922 to 1970 and best known for 190 short-subject films for [[Columbia Pictures]]. Their style was physical, farce-based slapstick. Moe Howard and Larry Fine were the constants, while six men appeared as the third stooge over the act's run. Curly Howard starred with them in more than 90 short comedies for Columbia from 1934 until a debilitating stroke in May 1946. Television syndication of the shorts in the early 1960s made the Stooges one of the most popular comedy acts of the period. Larry Fine suffered a paralyzing stroke in January 1970 while filming a pilot for a new TV series.

British daily national newspaper based in London and considered a newspaper of record in the United Kingdom. It began on January 1, 1785, as *The Daily Universal Register* and took its present name on January 1, 1788. It was the first newspaper to bear the name, which inspired many others around the world. Under editors Thomas Barnes and John Thadeus Delane, its influence in politics and in the [[City of London]] rose to great heights. Its sister paper, *The Sunday Times*, was founded in 1821, and the two titles have shared common ownership since 1966. The publisher, Times Media, has been a subsidiary of News UK since 1981. An American edition has been published since June 6, 2006, mainly in the [[New York City]] and [[Washington, D.C.]] areas. Its average daily circulation was 365,880 in March 2020.

Indian English-language daily newspaper, the oldest English-language newspaper in India. Its first edition appeared on November 3, 1838, as *The Bombay Times and Journal of Commerce*, and it took its present name in 1861. Under editor Robert Knight, the paper started India's first news agency, which served as the Indian agent for [[Reuters]]. It is the third-largest newspaper in India by circulation and is owned by Bennett, Coleman & Co., controlled by the Sahu Jain family. A 2021 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism rated it the most trusted news brand among English-speaking online news users in India. Since the 2000s it has been criticized for accepting payments in exchange for favorable coverage.

Ethno-nationalist conflict in [[Northern Ireland]] that lasted from the late 1960s to 1998. Unionists, mostly Ulster Protestants, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, while Irish nationalists, mostly Catholics, wanted a united Ireland. Republican and loyalist paramilitaries and British security forces fought a campaign of bombings, sectarian killings and riots. British troops were deployed after the August 1969 riots. More than 3,500 people were killed, 52% of them civilians. The [[Good Friday Agreement]] of 1998 ended the conflict and established power-sharing government, but sporadic violence has continued.

1998 American comedy-drama film directed by Peter Weir and written by Andrew Niccol. [[Jim Carrey]] stars as Truman Burbank, a man who is unaware that he lives on a soundstage in [[Los Angeles]] and that his life is the subject of a television show broadcast worldwide. [[Reality television|Reality television]] is one of the themes the film explores, along with simulated reality, existentialism, [[Surveillance]] and [[Privacy]]. Made for $60 million, it grossed $264 million worldwide and earned numerous nominations, including at the 71st Academy Awards. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 2025.

American television anthology series created and presented by [[Rod Serling]], broadcast on [[CBS]] from 1959 to 1964. Each episode presented a standalone story, often with a surprise ending and a moral, in which characters entered "the Twilight Zone." Serling wrote or co-wrote 92 of the series' 156 episodes and delivered the opening and closing narration of each. He chose a [[Science fiction|science fiction]] setting because he thought it gave him more freedom than realistic settings to express controversial ideas. The phrase "twilight zone" has entered the vernacular for surreal experiences.

American retired [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] known for the funerary, undead "Deadman" persona he played for [[WWE]]. Born Mark William Calaway, he began wrestling in 1987 and joined the World Wrestling Federation (now WWE) in 1990. He won 21 consecutive WrestleMania matches, known as The Streak, and headlined the event five times. He won the WWF/E Championship four times and the World Heavyweight Championship three times, and he won the Royal Rumble in 2007. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2022.

American investment management company, founded in 1975 and based in Malvern, Pennsylvania, near [[Philadelphia]]. With approximately $13.3 trillion in global assets under management as of 2025, it is the largest provider of mutual funds and the second-largest provider of exchange-traded funds after [[BlackRock]]'s iShares. Founder John C. Bogle, who had studied at [[Princeton University]], is credited with creating the first index fund for individual investors and became a leading advocate of low-cost investing. Vanguard is owned by the funds it manages and therefore by its customers. It is one of the Big Three index fund managers, along with BlackRock and State Street.

American rock band formed in [[New York City]] in 1964 that combined rock and roll with the avant-garde. Its provocative subject matter and experimentation helped shape [[Punk rock]], new wave and other genres, though it had little commercial success in its initial nine-year run. Pop artist [[Andy Warhol]] became its manager in 1966. Its debut album, *The Velvet Underground & Nico* (1967), sold poorly but was later hailed as one of the greatest albums in music history. The band dissolved shortly after its final album in 1973. Its members reunited for well-received shows in 1993, and in 2004 *Rolling Stone* ranked the group 19th among its 100 Greatest Artists of All Time.

American siblings Lana and Lilly Wachowski, both trans women, who work as a writing and directing team. Their directing debut was *Bound* (1996), and they achieved fame with *The Matrix* (1999), which won them the Saturn Award for Best Director. They wrote and directed its sequels, *The Matrix Reloaded* and *The Matrix Revolutions* (both 2003). Their later works include *V for Vendetta* (2005), adapted from the graphic novel by [[Alan Moore]] and David Lloyd, *Speed Racer* (2008), *Cloud Atlas* (2012) and the [[Netflix]] series *Sense8* (2015–2018).

American post-apocalyptic horror drama television series developed by Frank Darabont and based on the comic book series by Robert Kirkman, Tony Moore and Charlie Adlard. Its ensemble follows survivors of a [[Zombie|zombie]] apocalypse who must also contend with rival human groups. It premiered on AMC on October 31, 2010, and ended after eleven seasons and 177 episodes on November 20, 2022. It was produced in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. From its third season it drew the most 18- to 49-year-old viewers of any cable or broadcast series, and it was nominated for a Golden Globe for Best Television Series – Drama. Its viewership declined in later seasons.

Eleventh studio album by the English rock band [[Pink Floyd]], released as a double album in 1979. A rock opera, it follows "Pink," a jaded rock star who builds a psychological wall of isolation around himself. [[Roger Waters]] conceived it during the band's 1977 tour and modeled the character on himself and Syd Barrett. The album topped the US charts for 15 weeks and reached number three in the UK. Its single "Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2" was Pink Floyd's only UK and US number-one single. With over 30 million copies sold, it is the second-best-selling Pink Floyd album, behind *The Dark Side of the Moon*.

Halloween broadcast of the radio series *The Mercury Theatre on the Air*, directed and narrated by [[Orson Welles]] on October 30, 1938, over the [[CBS]] Radio Network. It adapted [[H. G. Wells|H. G. Wells's]] novel in a realistic "breaking news" format, describing an alien invasion that included the fall of New York City. Some listeners were convinced that a real invasion was under way, though the scale of the panic is disputed. Widespread media outrage followed, with calls for regulation by the FCC. Welles apologized the next morning, and no punitive action was taken. The 23-year-old Welles gained a reputation as an innovative storyteller and "trickster."

Science fiction novel by English author [[H. G. Wells]], serialized in 1897 and published in book form in 1898. It depicts an attempted invasion of Earth by Martians with far greater intelligence and more advanced weapons than humans, who intend to conquer Earth because their own world has reached the "last stage of exhaustion." The narrator, a man in [[Surrey]], witnesses the invasion of [[London]], in which tripod war machines armed with heat rays overwhelm human forces. Wells said that the inspiration for the plot was the catastrophic effect of European colonization on the Aboriginal Tasmanians. The plot has been interpreted as a commentary on [[Evolution]], [[Imperialism]] and Victorian fears. Orson Welles's [[The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)|1938 radio adaptation]] caused a sensation.

American daily newspaper published in [[Washington, D.C.]], considered a newspaper of record in the United States. Founded in 1877 by Stilson Hutchins, it was purchased out of bankruptcy and revived by financier Eugene Meyer in 1933. Its 1971 printing of the Pentagon Papers helped spur opposition to the [[Vietnam War]]. Reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein investigated a break-in at the Democratic National Committee that led to the [[Watergate scandal]] and the 1974 resignation of President [[Richard Nixon]]. The newspaper has won 76 [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prizes]], second only to [[The New York Times]]. In 2013 the Graham family sold it to Nash Holdings, a holding company owned by [[Jeff Bezos]], for US$250 million. In 2025 its print subscribers fell below 100,000 for the first time in 55 years.

Poem by [[T. S. Eliot]], published in 1922 and regarded as a central work of modernist poetry. The 434-line poem first appeared in the October 1922 issue of Eliot's magazine *The Criterion* in Britain and in the November issue of *The Dial* in the United States. It has no single narrative and shifts abruptly between voices, places and times, drawing on [[Ovid]], the legend of the Fisher King and Dante's *Divine Comedy*. [[Ezra Pound]] heavily revised it, reducing an original draft of more than 1,000 lines. Critics were initially divided over its obscurity, but it became one of the most influential poems of the 20th century.

Treatise on political economy by Scottish economist [[Adam Smith]], published on March 9, 1776. Smith argued that national wealth arises from productive labor and the division of labor rather than from accumulated gold, and he criticized the [[Feudalism|feudal]] and mercantilist policies of European states that restricted free exchange. His metaphor of an "invisible hand" described how self-interested individuals in a free market unintentionally promote the community's welfare. He also criticized slavery, primogeniture and imperial military expenditure. Although Smith did not use the term [[Capitalism]], the book became a foundational work of [[Liberalism|economic liberalism]]. [[Karl Marx]] called it "the true Bible of the classical political economy of the 18th century."

Canadian singer, songwriter and record producer whose stage name is The Weeknd. His light falsetto and dark, cinematic music videos are central to an alternative R&B sound that he blended with pop on later albums. He released three mixtapes in 2011, and his albums *Beauty Behind the Madness* (2015) and *Starboy* (2016) both debuted atop the US Billboard 200. *After Hours* (2020) featured "Blinding Lights," the best-performing song in the history of the Billboard Hot 100 and the most-streamed song on [[Spotify]]. He has won four [[Grammy Awards]] and co-created the [[HBO]] series *The Idol*.

Collection of two books of [[Fugue|fugues]] and preludes for keyboard by [[Johann Sebastian Bach]], with one prelude and fugue in each of the 24 major and minor keys. The first book, dated 1722, was compiled during Bach's appointment in Köthen. Twenty years later, in 1742, he compiled the second book while in [[Leipzig]]. The title alludes to well-tempered tuning, which allows music to be played in every key on a single instrument such as the [[Harpsichord]]. The work is a comprehensive guide to [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]], harmony and keyboard technique, and it is generally regarded as one of the most important works in the history of classical music.

American political drama television series created by [[Aaron Sorkin]], broadcast on [[NBC]] from 1999 to 2006. It is set mainly in the West Wing of the [[White House]] during the fictional two-term Democratic administration of President Josiah Bartlet, played by [[Martin Sheen]]. Its ensemble included [[Allison Janney]]. Sorkin, who wrote or co-wrote 85 of the first 88 episodes, left after the fourth season, and the ratings declined afterward. The series won 26 Primetime Emmy Awards, including four consecutive wins for Outstanding Drama Series from 2000 to 2003, and many publications have ranked it among the greatest television shows of all time.

English rock band formed in [[London]] in 1964. Its classic lineup of Roger Daltrey, [[Pete Townshend]], John Entwistle and Keith Moon was known for explosive live performances and for the rock opera, as in *Tommy* (1969) and *Quadrophenia* (1973). The band performed at [[Woodstock]] and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1990. After Moon died in 1978, Kenney Jones replaced him, and the group officially split in 1983. The members reunited intermittently, including for [[Live Aid]] in 1985. Daltrey and Townshend ended their touring career with a farewell tour in 2025.
